subject: lion
pitch: A proud old lion resting with his head held high. A huge shaggy mane fading from golden blond at the face to dark chocolate at the edges, a tawny body with a pale cream belly and muzzle, amber eyes, a broad black nose, a scar across one eyebrow, big padded paws and a long tail ending in a dark tuft.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a lion model in TypeScript using the SDK, working out realistic proportions—about 2.5 meters nose to tail, 1.2 meters at the shoulder—with the coordinate conventions in mind, aiming for a resting pose with the head held high.

I'm thinking through the sphinx-like resting posture: haunches tucked on the ground, chest raised, forelegs extended forward, head lifted. I'm sketching out body segment lengths along the Z-axis—nose around z=1.3, tail to z=-1.6, with the chest height around 0.95m—to make sure the proportions read naturally for a lion in this pose.

Now I'm working out the joint hierarchy, starting with a root joint at the hips and building a spine chain from pelvis up through the chest, figuring out how polyline knots map to joint counts along that chain.

I'm planning the full skeleton tree instead: hips as root, then chest, neck, head, and jaw joints each parented to the previous, placing their positions and direction vectors to get a proud, forward-leaning posture, and thinking through the jaw's hinge axis for mouth movement.

I'll build the mouth as a separate upper and lower jaw so it can open, add small rounded ears attached to the head, then set up leg chains for the forelegs using shoulder, elbow, wrist, and paw joints with the "leg" role, positioning them for a classic sphinx pose with legs extended forward and elbows bent on the floor.

I'm estimating joint positions for the shoulder, elbow, wrist, and paw and checking the segment distances come out close to the intended bone lengths, then considering whether to connect them with simple rigid rods between joints versus tapered capsules for a more natural limb shape.

For bending parts like the neck and tail I'll use smooth sweeps along chains, while the mane needs a different approach — likely feathery card textures with an SVG tuft shape tinted by a gradient Paint that fades from golden near the face to darker chocolate at the edges.

The texture decode timing matters since svg() textures fill asynchronously, but since this runs in-browser rather than Node, that's not a real concern here. I'm also considering mixing in some cone-like spikes alongside the mane cards to give a shaggier, more textured look overall.

For the mane coloring, I'm defining a Paint function that blends gold near the face center to dark chocolate toward the edges, based on radial distance from a head-center point, and having cards sample this paint directly at their root position. Then I'm generating frame points around the head/neck on an ellipsoid-like ring, with outward-facing directions, and feeding those into the card generator with a lean angle and cross-hatching for volume.

Now I'm adjusting the mane's flow direction to sweep back and down rather than straight out, adding randomized spin and variation via a seeded RNG, and binding the cards rigidly to the head joint. I'm also reconsidering the coverage area -- since a lion's mane extends past the head into the neck and chest, I'm planning the card ring to wrap around that broader shell while excluding the frontal face region where the direction vector points too far forward.

For the color fade, I'm thinking through how to map the golden-to-chocolate gradient onto the mane cards based on proximity to the face center versus the outer rim, testing a couple of ways to define that face-center point and radius so cards near the face read as gold and cards farther out darken toward chocolate.

Checking module exports...

So paint, mottle, stripes, gradient, noise, and other color utilities are all exported with no naming conflicts since `mix` resolves explicitly to the paint version. I'm thinking through how to use these paints for the creature's body — countershading with a tawny tone, a gradient for the mane — keeping in mind textures bake to a shared 1024px canvas with a density limit across all painted parts.

For the body itself, I'm planning a loft along the torso from hips to chest, using stations with position, width, and height, and binding the sweep to the hip and chest joints so the path's weighting follows bone order correctly rather than defaulting to nearest-joint weighting.

Beyond the body, I'm sketching the full lion out of primitives: a loft/capsule body, a head with a snout box, mane cards, tapered capsule legs with sphere or box paws, a tail sweep with a tufted end, amber sphere eyes with black pupils, and a dark nose shape. For the scar across the brow, I'm weighing a thin capsule or rod in a darker reddish-brown versus a painted stripe mapped onto the head's surface coordinates, leaning toward the simpler geometric capsule approach.

Now I'm considering using a decal instead -- rendering an SVG texture of a jagged scar line with a transparent background and projecting it onto the head surface at the brow point, using a direction and position to orient it correctly, with alpha-tested transparency so only the scar mark shows through.

I'm also weighing the complexity this adds versus a simpler approach: computing the scar's surface position analytically if the head is built from a sphere with known center and radius, letting me place a thin rod directly on the calculated surface point rather than relying on decals or raycasting.

Actually, using a decal makes more sense here — it's a clean way to layer small details onto a simple shape. I'd apply it to the head part as the target surface, with a position near the brow and a direction vector pointing outward from the face toward the viewer, sized small enough to read as a scar mark.

For the scar itself, I'm drawing a jagged diagonal line in SVG, a few connected segments crossing the brow at an angle, styled in a dark reddish-brown with rounded strokes so it reads as a healed scar rather than a cut. I'm matching the decal's aspect ratio to the SVG's viewbox so the line doesn't stretch unnaturally, keeping the overall size small and proportioned to the face.

Now I'm thinking through the body's paint scheme: a countershaded tawny back fading to a pale cream belly, which works naturally for the sphinx pose since the raised chest shows the lighter underside. The muzzle gets its own cream-colored part separate from the golden-tawny forehead, with a black nose, and the mane transitions from gold to chocolate using painted card geometry.

I'm now mapping out the mane cards so they wrap around the sides and back of the head and down the neck, leaving the face clear, and placing the amber eyes with small black pupils onto the head's forward surface.

To position eyes and other features precisely, I'm defining a helper that projects a direction onto the ellipsoid surface using scaled radii, so I can compute consistent surface points for eyes, pupils, and the nose without hand-calculating each coordinate.

Now I'm placing the muzzle, nose, and lower jaw as separate shaped parts attached to the jaw bone, flattening the nose into a broad black shape and sizing the lower jaw ellipsoid to sit under the muzzle at the hinge joint — explicitly binding each part to the "jaw" bone rather than relying on automatic nearest-joint detection.

For the ears, I'm thinking of small flattened tawny spheres positioned on the sides of the head's top, but I'm wary that the mane cards starting further out on the head shell might cover them if the ears sit too far inward — so I'll keep them small and partially visible through the mane rather than cutting them entirely. Now I'm shifting to laying out the overall sphinx pose, working out world coordinates for the torso starting from the hips toward the chest, with the back and belly heights needing to sit low and close to the ground for the characteristic sphinx posture.

I'm sketching loft stations along the spine from rump to chest, specifying center height, width, and height at each cross-section so the belly sags appropriately while the chest lifts higher toward the raised forelegs, checking that the lowest points barely touch the ground without sinking too far.

Now I'm placing the rump end with rounded loft caps, then positioning the head, neck, and mane: head centered around [0, 1.02, 0.86] with muzzle protruding forward, and a smooth neck sweep connecting chest to head with tapering radius hidden under mane bulk.

Working out the joint hierarchy next: hips as root, chest, neck, and head joints with forward-upward orientation for the "held high" pose, then a jaw joint hinged near the back of the mouth so the lower jaw extends forward from the skull.

For the forelegs, I'm placing mirrored shoulder, elbow, wrist, and paw joints on the left side at specific coordinates, checking bone lengths stay consistent with the upper arm and forearm sizes, to get the classic sphinx pose with legs extended forward and paws flat on the ground.

I'm shaping the paws as tapered capsules from shoulder to elbow and elbow to wrist, then adding a padded paw ellipsoid with small toe bumps and tiny claw cones at the front, keeping the paw tawny-colored. Now I'm moving on to planning the hind leg joints starting with the hip.

For the hind legs, I'm positioning a sphinx-style haunch with the hip, knee, and ankle joints arranged so the thigh forms a large rounded capsule and the shin tapers down into a flat paw placed forward on the ground, adjusting the z-coordinates so the bent-knee pose reads correctly without overlapping the rump too much.

Now I'm planning the tail as a swept chain of joints curving back from the rump, dipping down, and ending in a dark tufted tip resting on the ground, using a chain of named joints with a tapering radius for the sweep.

Confirming the array radius works positionally with sweep, then thinking about the tail tuft design—using a teardrop-shaped hair strand SVG with a pointed tip, tinted dark brown, reused across the mane and tail cards with per-card color variation.

I'm thinking through mane strand sizing and card counts—around 60-200 double-sided cross cards for volume, staying well under triangle budgets. Cards use vertex colors with white tint over textures, and attach rigidly to the head bone, though I note this means mane over the neck/chest won't deform with neck movement.

So I decide to call the cards function twice separately, once bound to the head bone and once to the neck/chest bone, keeping the mane groups independent. For body coloring, I'm planning countershading with a tawny back and cream belly, and sketching out head paint with golden-tawny tones, cream muzzle, and amber eyes, leaving the face region open where the mane shell wraps around the sides and back of the head.

For the mane itself, I'm writing a gradient paint function that blends gold near the face through tawny into dark chocolate farther away, using distance from a face point and smoothstep interpolation with mix calls between color stops.

I'm checking that colors pass through the pipeline correctly: cards use this paint to push vertex colors through a linear-space conversion for sRGB correctness, and textured meshes multiply the map by white or a tint string like dark chocolate for the tail tuft, pulling in the right texture per distinct material group.

Now I'm moving to the body loft, which builds a smooth sweep across four stations with a countershade paint tinted by surface normal, bound to the hips and chest bones so weights blend correctly along the catmull-rom path connecting the station points.

I'm working out section geometry for the body sweep — using separate x/y radii per station to get an elliptical cross-section, and bumping up the polygon count to 12 sides so the body doesn't look too faceted.

For the neck, I'm lofting a similar tapered tube from chest to head with bone weights across chest, neck, and head joints, since the neck geometry doubles as the base for the mane.

For the head, I'm building it as a scaled sphere (an ellipsoid via non-uniform scale) bound to the head bone, relying on the paint system's chartify step to bake colors in world space so the transform doesn't break shading; I'm choosing a modest segment count to keep it low-poly but clean.

I'm deciding on color treatment for the head: using a normal-based countershade so the upper forehead reads golden-tawny while the lower jaw and muzzle areas shift toward cream, which pairs with a separate cream muzzle ellipsoid, a small flattened black nose, and a subtler cream lower-jaw shape positioned just beneath the muzzle.

I'm placing the eyes as small amber spheres on the head surface using normalized direction vectors toward the front-upper sides, with black pupil spheres sitting slightly in front of them, and adding a scar decal across one eyebrow by picking a brow-region surface point and projecting it along an outward normal direction.

I'm also reasoning through how the mane shell should wrap around the head and neck without covering the face — defining it as a larger ellipsoid shell offset from the head center, then filtering candidate hair-card directions (sampled via a Fibonacci sphere) to exclude the forward-facing region so the face, eyes, and brow scar stay visible while the top, sides, and back get full shaggy coverage, with a second lower cluster of cards flowing down toward the neck and chest.
